title: The Registry Saved Me
description:
You remembered being careful when you signed the jeonse contract.
Then news came: the landlord filed for bankruptcy.

Jeonse fraud warnings have been all over the news. But you have the stamp.

choices.text: Gather the fixed-date stamp documents and respond
choices.result_text:
Fixed-date stamp. Leasehold registration. The paperwork you filed that day protected everything.

Recognized as a priority creditor in the foreclosure proceedings. Full deposit returned.
You were grateful to the version of yourself who paid attention.

title: Jeonse Fraud — Too Close
description:
A text message: the landlord has filed for bankruptcy.
You should have gotten the fixed-date stamp at the community center back then.

Jeonse fraud is no longer something that happens to other people.

choices.text: Contact the Legal Aid Corporation and fight for what you can recover
choices.result_text:
Went to the Legal Aid Corporation. No fixed-date stamp means you're a junior creditor.

₩500,000 lost in the end — a partial recovery.
[One document. One trip to the community center. That's what it cost to protect ₩50M in deposit money. In Korea, jeonse fraud has cost thousands of people their life savings. The fixed-date stamp costs ₩600 to file, takes 10 minutes, and can be the only protection.]
Now you know it in your bones.

title: What the Dinner Left Behind
description:
The team leader called you over.
'Are you interested in leading the new project next quarter?'

Was it because you stayed until the end at that dinner? Or because of the actual work?
Maybe both.

choices.result_text:
'you'll do it.'

Did this opportunity come from the company dinner, or from your results?
In Korean workplaces, these two things are woven together.

choices.text: Say you'd rather wait until you're more ready
choices.result_text:
'you'd like to take it on when you're a bit more prepared.' Said it clearly.

The team leader nodded. Opportunities come to people who save them for the right moment too.
Decided to prepare for the next one.

title: What the Kkondae Said Back
description:
The team leader pulled you aside after hours.

'Oh no,' you thought. 'Here it comes.'

choices.result_text:
'What you said back then — I thought about it. You were right. Everyone else just lets it go these days.'

Not what you expected.
Saying what you actually think can move even a kkondae — sometimes.

title: The Weight of Accumulated Overtime
description:
Eye-contact overtime has piled up.
The body starts sending signals.

Stiff neck, blurry screen. On Sunday nights, a tight chest at the thought of going in.

choices.text: Decide to start drawing the line
choices.result_text:
'From now on, I leave when the work is done.' Decided internally.

[Nunchi overtime: overtime performed not because there's actual work, but because no one wants to be seen leaving before the boss. A distinctly Korean workplace phenomenon — the cost isn't just time, it's accumulated health damage.]
The body won against the office. The line is yours to draw.

Just a little more. Just a little more.

The 'little mores' piled up until the body protested. Indigestion. Sleepless nights.
Endurance has limits. You'd already passed yours by some distance.

title: Tax Refund Arrives
description:
Hometax notification: refund amount confirmed.

The careful deduction work paid off.

choices.result_text:
₩150,000 deposited.

Money the government owed me. The difference between knowing the system and not.
People who work this every year keep a little more — every year.

title: Small Trust in the Goshiwon
description:
The woman next door stopped you in the hallway.

'You've been so good with the recycling lately. Thank you.'
You'd barely noticed her. Turns out she noticed you.

choices.result_text:
We learned each other's names.

You have a neighbor in the goshiwon now. Small trust built from something small.
[Recycling rules in Korea are strict and specific: separate plastic, cans, paper, styrofoam, glass, food waste — each with its own designated bin and day. Rinsing bottles, removing labels — it's genuinely complex. But everyone does it, because the social pressure to comply is real. The unwritten compact that makes this country's density work.]
